newsitem.title: UK: Britain turns up heat on France over truck blockade.
newsitem.headline: Britain turns up heat on France over truck blockade.

text.p: Britain turned up the heat on France on Wednesday to secure the release of hundreds of British truck drivers caught up in a strike by French drivers, that has paralysed much cross-channel traffic.

"We've been in touch with the French to make it clear we think they have an obligation firstly to end this dispute as speedily as possible and secondly to meet compensation claims for damage done to perishable goods," Prime Minister John Major told reporters.
"I very much hope they will be able to end the strike --. It's a matter for them and not us," he said.
Secretary of State for Transport George Young met British truck and freight organisations and vowed to step up pressure to help drivers stranded by the 10-day strike over pay and conditions.

Many British drivers have been living for days in their cabs, running out of money, food and patience. Others are trying to avoid the chaos by taking an alternative route across the Channel via Zeebrugge in Belgium.

After meeting representatives of the Freight Transport Association and the Road Haulage Association, Young said the main tasks now were to extricate British drivers from the blockade and to pursue compensation.

"I'm sending a telegram to my opposite number asking for fresh initiatives to be taken to ensure that the British lorry drivers are freed from the blockade," he told the British Broadcasting Corporation.
"Full and fair compensation should be given for the losses incurred in this dispute," Young said.
He said he was also asking the French government to lift restrictions on driving trucks on Sunday and on drivers' hours so British drivers can get home once the blockade is ended.
The Road Haulage Association, representing some 10,000 hauliers, said Young was considering seeking support from fellow European Union states to prevent any repeat of the situation.
Freight Transport Association spokesman Geoff Dossetter said that reports of some vehicles being allowed through at Calais turned out to be false and the situation had not changed.
On the British side, about 800-900 vehicles were queueing at Dover on Wednesday morning to get to Zeebrugge, he said.
P&O European Ferries said freight was being diverted to Zeebrugge, where three freight ships operate regular crossings.

"What we've now done is also taken one of the ships from Dover-Calais to bolster the ships on the Zeebrugge route, so we're managing to clear all the freight from Dover through into Belgium," P&O spokesman Ian Todd said.

"All the French channel ports are blocked by the strikers," he said. "Zeebrugge may be better for some drivers going into Germany and Eastern Europe, because it is a shorter run. But Calais is only a 75-minute crossing. It takes four hours to Zeebrugge."
Road Haulage Association spokesman Sydney Balgarnie said that sending vehicles through Zeebrugge involved longer turnaround times than on the much shorter Calais route and would cost more.
The lorry drivers' organisations said the French action would have little impact on road haulage within Britain, but there could be some problems with supplies from Europe.
"It is a separate market to an extent in as much as the vehicles that are involved in international traffic are on that sort of traffic all the time," Balgarnie said.
